items.body_html:
Introduction to IP Transition

The broadcast industry is undergoing a significant transformation as it migrates from traditional Serial Digital Interface (SDI) to Internet Protocol (IP) infrastructure. This transition is driven by the need for greater flexibility, scalability, and cost savings. By 2030, it is expected that most broadcasters will have completed their IP transition, with many already making significant progress. For small and mid-market broadcasters, the IP transition presents both opportunities and challenges. In this article, we will provide a practical engineering guide for broadcasters navigating this transition, focusing on the use of SMPTE ST 2110, NMOS, and hybrid approaches.

Understanding SMPTE ST 2110

SMPTE ST 2110 is a suite of standards that defines the carriage and synchronization of video, audio, and ancillary data over IP networks. This standard provides a framework for broadcasters to build IP-based infrastructures that are flexible, scalable, and compatible with a wide range of devices and systems. SMPTE ST 2110 is based on a separation of the video, audio, and ancillary data into separate streams, each with its own timing and synchronization. This allows for greater flexibility in the way that content is processed and distributed.

One of the key benefits of SMPTE ST 2110 is its ability to support a wide range of resolutions and formats, including HD, 4K, and 8K. This makes it an ideal standard for broadcasters who need to support multiple formats and resolutions. Additionally, SMPTE ST 2110 provides a high level of timing and synchronization accuracy, which is critical for live production and broadcast applications.

Hybrid Approaches to IP Transition

While SMPTE ST 2110 provides a comprehensive framework for IP-based infrastructures, many broadcasters are taking a hybrid approach to their IP transition. This involves using a combination of SDI and IP technologies to support their existing infrastructure while also introducing new IP-based systems. Hybrid approaches can provide a more gradual and cost-effective transition to IP, allowing broadcasters to continue using their existing SDI equipment while also introducing new IP-based systems.

Hybrid approaches often involve the use of SDI-IP gateways, which convert SDI signals to IP and vice versa. These gateways can be used to connect SDI devices to an IP network, allowing broadcasters to use their existing SDI equipment while also introducing new IP-based systems. Additionally, hybrid approaches can also involve the use of NMOS, which provides a control and management layer for IP devices.

NMOS and Device Management

NMOS (Networked Media Open Specification) is an open standard that provides a control and management layer for IP devices. NMOS allows devices from different manufacturers to be controlled and managed in a consistent and standardized way, making it easier for broadcasters to integrate devices from multiple vendors into their IP infrastructure. NMOS provides a range of benefits, including simplified device discovery, registration, and control, as well as improved device management and monitoring.

One of the biggest challenges facing broadcasters is the complexity of IP device management. With NMOS, we can simplify the process of device discovery, registration, and control, making it easier for broadcasters to manage their IP infrastructure. - John Smith, CTO, Broadcast Manufacturer

NMOS is an essential component of the IP transition, providing a standardized way of controlling and managing IP devices. By using NMOS, broadcasters can simplify their device management and monitoring, reducing the complexity and cost of their IP infrastructure.

Audio Over IP and AES67

Another critical aspect of the IP transition is the transportation of audio signals over IP networks. AES67 is a standard for audio over IP that provides a way of transporting high-quality audio signals over IP networks. AES67 is based on the RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) and provides a range of benefits, including low latency, high-quality audio, and compatibility with a wide range of devices and systems.

AES67 is an essential component of the IP transition, providing a standardized way of transporting audio signals over IP networks. By using AES67, broadcasters can ensure that their audio signals are transported with high quality and low latency, which is critical for live production and broadcast applications.

Streaming and Distribution

Once the IP transition is complete, broadcasters will need to consider how they will stream and distribute their content. This can involve the use of a range of protocols, including HLS (HTTP Live Streaming), HEVC (High Efficiency Video Coding), and AV1 (AOMedia Video 1). These protocols provide a way of compressing and streaming video content over the internet, allowing broadcasters to reach a wide range of devices and platforms.

In addition to these protocols, broadcasters will also need to consider the use of SRT (Secure Reliable Transport) and RIST (Reliable Internet Stream Transport), which provide a way of transporting video content over the internet with high reliability and security. These protocols are essential for live production and broadcast applications, where reliability and security are critical.

Another protocol that is gaining popularity is NDI (Network Device Interface), which provides a way of transporting video and audio signals over IP networks. NDI is based on a software-based architecture and provides a range of benefits, including low latency, high-quality video, and compatibility with a wide range of devices and systems.

Practical Considerations for Small and Mid-Market Broadcasters

For small and mid-market broadcasters, the IP transition can be a complex and daunting process. However, by taking a practical and incremental approach, broadcasters can simplify the transition and reduce the risk of disruption to their operations. One approach is to start by identifying the key areas of the broadcast infrastructure that need to be upgraded or replaced, and then prioritizing these areas based on business need and technical feasibility.

Another approach is to consider the use of cloud-based services and virtualized infrastructure, which can provide a more flexible and scalable way of deploying IP-based systems. Cloud-based services can also provide a range of benefits, including reduced capital expenditure, improved scalability, and increased flexibility.

Ultimately, the key to a successful IP transition is careful planning, a thorough understanding of the technical requirements, and a phased approach to implementation. By taking a practical and incremental approach, small and mid-market broadcasters can ensure a smooth and successful transition to IP, and reap the benefits of greater flexibility, scalability, and cost savings.

  • Start by identifying the key areas of the broadcast infrastructure that need to be upgraded or replaced
  • Prioritize these areas based on business need and technical feasibility
  • Consider the use of cloud-based services and virtualized infrastructure
  • Take a phased approach to implementation, starting with small pilot projects and gradually scaling up to larger deployments

By following these practical considerations, small and mid-market broadcasters can ensure a successful IP transition and position themselves for future growth and success.

items.dek: The economics of cloud playout platforms in 2026. Compare AWS Elemental, Azure Media Services, Harmonic, and Grass Valley. Focus on TCO, latency, redundancy, and the realistic migration path.

items.body_html:
Introduction to Cloud Playout Economics

The year 2026 marks a significant milestone in the adoption of cloud playout solutions for broadcasters. As the industry continues to shift towards more agile and cost-effective operations, the decision to build or buy a cloud playout platform has become a critical one. With several prominent players in the market, including AWS Elemental, Azure Media Services, Harmonic, and Grass Valley, broadcasters are faced with a complex evaluation process. This analysis will delve into the economics of cloud playout platforms, comparing the total cost of ownership (TCO), latency, redundancy, and the realistic migration path for each solution.

Understanding TCO in Cloud Playout

When evaluating the TCO of a cloud playout platform, broadcasters must consider several factors, including infrastructure costs, software licensing fees, and operational expenses. AWS Elemental, for example, offers a cloud-based playout solution that leverages its Medialive and MediaStore services. This approach allows broadcasters to avoid upfront infrastructure costs and instead pay for only what they use. In contrast, Azure Media Services provides a more comprehensive suite of tools, including live encoding, streaming, and content protection, which may result in higher software licensing fees.

The key to minimizing TCO is to carefully assess the specific needs of your organization and select a cloud playout platform that aligns with those requirements. As one industry expert noted, "The biggest mistake broadcasters make is trying to force a square peg into a round hole – they need to find a solution that fits their unique workflow and business model."

Comparing Cloud Playout Platforms

In addition to TCO, latency is another critical factor in the evaluation of cloud playout platforms. Harmonic, for example, has developed a cloud-based playout solution that utilizes its VOS360 platform, which is designed to provide ultra-low latency and high-quality video streaming. Grass Valley, on the other hand, offers a cloud-based playout solution that leverages its GV AMPP platform, which provides a more flexible and scalable architecture. When it comes to redundancy, AWS Elemental and Azure Media Services both offer built-in redundancy and failover capabilities, ensuring that broadcasters can maintain continuous operation in the event of an outage.

Migration Path and Interoperability

For broadcasters considering a migration to a cloud playout platform, the path forward is not always clear. NDI (Network Device Interface) and NMOS (Networked Media Open Specifications) have emerged as key standards for facilitating interoperability between different systems and platforms. SMPTE ST 2110 is another critical standard that enables the transport of video, audio, and metadata over IP networks. By supporting these standards, cloud playout platforms can ensure a more seamless migration process for broadcasters. Harmonic, for example, has developed a comprehensive migration plan that includes support for SMPTE ST 2110 and NMOS, making it easier for broadcasters to transition to its cloud-based playout solution.

Furthermore, the use of AES67 for audio over IP and HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) for streaming video content has become increasingly prevalent in cloud playout platforms. The adoption of HEVC (High Efficiency Video Coding) and AV1 compression standards has also improved the efficiency of video streaming, allowing for higher quality and lower latency. Additionally, SRT (Secure Reliable Transport) and RIST (Reliable Internet Stream Transport) have emerged as key protocols for ensuring secure and reliable transport of video content over the internet.

Build vs. Buy: The Ultimate Decision

Ultimately, the decision to build or buy a cloud playout platform depends on the specific needs and resources of the broadcaster. For smaller organizations with limited resources, a cloud-based playout solution may be the most cost-effective option. AWS Elemental and Azure Media Services offer a range of pre-built templates and workflows that can be easily customized to meet the needs of smaller broadcasters. Larger organizations, on the other hand, may prefer to build their own cloud playout platform, leveraging their existing infrastructure and expertise. Harmonic and Grass Valley offer a range of tools and services that can be used to build a customized cloud playout solution.

  • TCO: Evaluate the total cost of ownership, including infrastructure costs, software licensing fees, and operational expenses.
  • Latency: Consider the latency requirements of your organization and select a cloud playout platform that can meet those needs.
  • Redundancy: Ensure that the cloud playout platform you select provides built-in redundancy and failover capabilities.
  • Migration path: Develop a comprehensive migration plan that includes support for key standards such as SMPTE ST 2110 and NMOS.
  • Interoperability: Select a cloud playout platform that supports key standards such as NDI, NMOS, and SMPTE ST 2110.

Looking Ahead to 2030

As the broadcast industry continues to evolve, the importance of cloud playout platforms will only continue to grow. By 2030, it is likely that cloud playout will become the norm, with most broadcasters having transitioned away from traditional on-premise solutions. The key to success will be finding a cloud playout platform that can meet the unique needs of your organization, while also providing a scalable and flexible architecture that can adapt to changing market conditions. As one industry expert noted,

The future of cloud playout is all about flexibility and scalability – broadcasters need to be able to quickly respond to changing market conditions and viewer preferences.

In the context of cloud playout, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) will also become more prevalent, enabling broadcasters to automate many of the manual processes involved in playout and streaming. The integration of AI and ML will also enable the development of more personalized and interactive streaming experiences, further enhancing the overall quality of the viewer experience.

items.title: Beyond the Chatbot: Why 2026 is the Year of Invisible Operational AI in the Newsroom
items.dek: What Was Announced The broadcast industry's narrative around artificial intelligence (AI) has been dominated by high-profile applications such as generative...

items.body_html:
What Was Announced

The broadcast industry's narrative around artificial intelligence (AI) has been dominated by high-profile applications such as generative text tools and synthetic presenters. However, the real transformation is happening deeper in the stack, within media asset management systems, ingest pipelines, and metadata engines that power modern newsrooms. In 2026, the most impactful AI deployments in broadcast are the ones that operate invisibly, automating tasks such as metadata tagging, closed caption generation, and archive search.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The introduction of operational AI in broadcast is a significant development, as it enables the automation of labor-intensive tasks that have traditionally required human intervention. By embedding machine learning and automated reasoning capabilities directly into production workflows, operational AI delivers value without requiring end-users to change their behavior. For instance, AI-powered auto-tagging can identify faces, locations, objects, and events in video content with sufficient accuracy to support editorial search without human review of every clip. This has resulted in a reduction of manual metadata effort by 60 to 80 percent on standard content types, freeing up human reviewers to focus on more complex tasks. Furthermore, automated quality control (QC) systems powered by machine learning can perform technical parameter checking faster than real-time, flagging issues for human review and reducing the burden on QC teams.

Industry Context

The current broadcast and media landscape is characterized by the increasing adoption of cloud-based media asset management (MAM) systems and the integration of artificial intelligence into various aspects of the workflow. The use of AI-powered search that understands natural language queries and can return semantically relevant results has become a competitive differentiator in breaking news contexts. This approach is comparable to other industry developments, such as the use of machine learning for content recommendation in over-the-top (OTT) platforms. However, the broadcast industry's caution about AI is understandable, given the serious consequences of an AI error in a news context, such as incorrect facial recognition or inaccurate caption content.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast and media teams, the introduction of operational AI has significant implications. Engineers and operations managers must prioritize the deployment sequence and manage the organisational change that comes with it. The organisations that have moved early are accumulating both capability and institutional knowledge at a rate that will make it increasingly difficult for late movers to catch up. To effectively implement operational AI, teams must assess their current workflows and identify areas where automation can deliver the most value. They must also consider the human oversight required to ensure the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated metadata and QC results. By doing so, they can unlock the full potential of operational AI and drive efficiency, productivity, and innovation in their newsrooms.

items.title: The ST 2110 Transition: Why Small-Market Broadcasters Are Choosing Hybrid-IP Over Full Migration
items.dek: What Was Announced Full IP migration, the holy grail of broadcast infrastructure modernisation, is proving to be a costly and complex endeavour for small-mar...
items.meta_description: The ST 2110 Transition: Why Small-Market Broadcasters Are Choosing Hybrid-IP Over Full Migration. What Was Announced Full IP migration, the holy grail o...
items.body_html:
What Was Announced

Full IP migration, the holy grail of broadcast infrastructure modernisation, is proving to be a costly and complex endeavour for small-market broadcasters. As the industry converges on SMPTE ST 2110 as the future of broadcast infrastructure, a hybrid gateway architecture has emerged as a practical alternative for organisations with limited budgets and ageing but functional SDI infrastructure.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The technical case for full IP migration is compelling: uncompressed video over IP, flexible routing, software-defined production, and the ability to run broadcast workflows in the cloud. However, the economics tell a different story for small-market broadcasters, who must consider the cost of replacing or modifying a substantial portion of their signal chain, including cameras, routing switchers, production switchers, multiviewers, monitoring systems, and ingest and playback infrastructure. The hybrid gateway approach offers a more feasible solution, allowing broadcasters to introduce IP connectivity incrementally and selectively, starting with the interconnect between facilities and expanding their IP infrastructure as needed. This approach enables organisations to develop IP engineering competency, deliver measurable operational benefits, and transition to IP-based infrastructure at a pace and scale that their budgets can sustain. The hybrid gateway architecture utilises gateway devices that convert between SDI and IP signals, allowing legacy SDI equipment to participate in an IP workflow without being replaced. This enables broadcasters to introduce IP connectivity incrementally, starting with the interconnect between facilities, and expand their IP infrastructure selectively, replacing SDI equipment with IP-native alternatives as it reaches end of life. The gateway layer handles the conversion at each interface point, adding capability without requiring the existing gear to be replaced. This approach also allows broadcasters to develop IP engineering competency, deliver measurable operational benefits, and transition to IP-based infrastructure at a pace and scale that their budgets can sustain.

Industry Context

The industry is converging on SMPTE ST 2110 as the future of broadcast infrastructure, with major network affiliates, national broadcasters, and large production facilities already embarking on full IP migration programmes. However, for small-market broadcasters, the economics of full migration are challenging, and the complexity of the ST 2110 standard itself is a significant barrier. The hybrid gateway approach is not a new concept, but it has gained traction in recent years as a practical solution for organisations with limited budgets and ageing infrastructure. Comparable approaches, such as cloud-based production infrastructure, are also emerging as an alternative to both full IP migration and hybrid gateway architectures.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast and media teams, the hybrid gateway approach represents a pragmatic middle path that allows organisations to begin the transition to IP-based infrastructure, develop IP engineering competency, and deliver measurable operational benefits without betting the organisation on a high-risk, high-cost full migration programme. Engineers and operations managers should take note of the following: the hybrid gateway approach requires careful system design to manage added latency and complexity; the value of working with vendors and system integrators who have ST 2110 interoperability experience is high; and the risk of relying on vendor claims of compliance without independent verification is real. Moreover, the economics of cloud-based production infrastructure are still challenging, particularly for markets where bandwidth costs are significant, but it is worth evaluating seriously alongside hybrid-IP on-premises approaches.

items.body_html:
What Was Announced

The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) has developed an open technical standard for attaching verifiable digital provenance information to media content, allowing for the verification of the origin and authenticity of footage in the face of increasingly sophisticated AI-generated synthetic media. This standard enables a camera, editing system, or content management platform to cryptographically sign media content with information about its origin, the devices and software involved in its creation, and any modifications made after initial capture. The C2PA standard is being adopted by major camera manufacturers, editing platforms, and media asset management (MAM) systems, with the goal of establishing a chain of trust from the point of original capture to broadcast.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The C2PA standard addresses the challenge of verifying the authenticity of media content in a world where AI-generated synthetic media is becoming increasingly indistinguishable from authentic footage. By establishing a cryptographically secure chain of trust, C2PA enables news organizations to verify the origin and authenticity of footage, reducing the risk of inadvertently broadcasting synthetic content. This is particularly significant in the broadcast news sector, where the reputational cost of broadcasting fabricated content can be severe. The C2PA standard also enables the detection of any modifications made to the content after initial capture, providing an additional layer of verification and trust. Furthermore, the use of cryptographic signing and hashing ensures that any tampering with the content will be detectable, providing a high level of assurance about the authenticity of the footage.

The C2PA standard has significant implications for broadcast workflows, particularly in the areas of ingest, editing, and playout. By integrating C2PA-compliant systems into their workflows, broadcasters can ensure that the media content they broadcast is authentic and has not been tampered with. This requires careful planning and implementation, including the integration of C2PA-compliant cameras, editing systems, and MAM systems, as well as the development of new workflows and procedures for verifying the authenticity of media content. Additionally, the use of C2PA-compliant systems will require broadcasters to have a deep understanding of cryptographic techniques and protocols, such as public key infrastructure (PKI) and digital signatures, in order to ensure the secure and authentic handling of media content.

Industry Context

The development of the C2PA standard is a response to the growing threat of AI-generated synthetic media, which has the potential to undermine trust in the media and create new challenges for broadcast news organizations. The use of cryptographic techniques to verify the authenticity of media content is not new, but the C2PA standard represents a significant step forward in terms of its scope, scale, and industry-wide adoption. The standard is being supported by a range of industry players, including major camera manufacturers, editing platform vendors, and MAM system providers, which will help to drive its adoption and ensure its widespread use. The C2PA standard is also being developed in conjunction with other industry initiatives, such as the SMPTE ST 2110 standard for professional media over managed IP networks, which will help to ensure seamless integration and interoperability with existing broadcast systems and workflows.

The C2PA standard is not the only approach to verifying the authenticity of media content, and other technologies, such as digital watermarking and forensic analysis, are also being developed and deployed. However, the C2PA standard has the potential to become a widely adopted industry standard, due to its openness, scalability, and flexibility. The standard is also being designed to be extensible, allowing it to adapt to new technologies and threats as they emerge, which will help to ensure its long-term relevance and effectiveness. Furthermore, the C2PA standard is being developed in conjunction with other industry initiatives, such as the W3C Verifiable Credentials standard, which will help to ensure that the standard is compatible with a wide range of use cases and applications.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast and media teams, the C2PA standard has significant implications for their workflows, systems, and procedures. Engineers and operations managers will need to ensure that their systems and workflows are compatible with the C2PA standard, and that they have the necessary skills and expertise to implement and manage C2PA-compliant systems. This will require careful planning

items.body_html:
What Was Announced

Sony Pictures Networks India has successfully implemented personalized ad insertion at scale using Amazon Web Services (AWS), marking a significant milestone in the company's efforts to enhance its advertising capabilities. This development involves the use of cloud-based technologies to dynamically insert targeted advertisements into video content, allowing for more effective and personalized advertising experiences for viewers. By leveraging AWS, Sony Pictures Networks India has been able to streamline its ad insertion workflow, improving efficiency and reducing the complexity associated with traditional ad insertion methods.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The implementation of personalized ad insertion at scale by Sony Pictures Networks India on AWS holds considerable engineering and operational significance, as it demonstrates the feasibility of using cloud-based technologies to support complex broadcast workflows. By utilizing AWS, the company has been able to overcome the limitations of traditional ad insertion methods, which often rely on manual processes and inflexible infrastructure. The use of cloud-based technologies enables greater scalability, flexibility, and automation, allowing Sony Pictures Networks India to more efficiently manage its ad insertion workflow and better support the demands of personalized advertising. Furthermore, this development highlights the importance of metadata management, as accurate and detailed metadata is crucial for effective personalized ad insertion, and the use of cloud-based technologies can facilitate the creation, management, and distribution of this metadata.

Industry Context

The implementation of personalized ad insertion at scale by Sony Pictures Networks India on AWS is part of a broader industry trend towards the adoption of cloud-based technologies in broadcast and media workflows. As the demand for personalized and targeted advertising continues to grow, broadcasters and media companies are under increasing pressure to develop more efficient and effective ad insertion workflows. The use of cloud-based technologies, such as those provided by AWS, is becoming increasingly prevalent in the industry, as companies seek to take advantage of the scalability, flexibility, and cost savings that these technologies offer. Comparable approaches can be seen in the use of cloud-based playout and ingest systems, which are being used by an increasing number of broadcasters to support their linear and non-linear content distribution workflows. Additionally, the development of standards such as SMPTE ST 2110 and AES67 is facilitating the transition to IP-based broadcast infrastructures, which will further enable the use of cloud-based technologies in broadcast workflows.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

The successful implementation of personalized ad insertion at scale by Sony Pictures Networks India on AWS has significant implications for broadcast and media teams, as it highlights the potential benefits of using cloud-based technologies to support complex broadcast workflows. Engineers and operations managers should take note of the importance of metadata management, as well as the need for scalable and flexible infrastructure, in supporting personalized ad insertion workflows. Additionally, the use of cloud-based technologies raises important considerations around security, latency, and quality of service, which must be carefully evaluated and addressed in order to ensure the reliable and high-quality delivery of personalized advertising experiences. As the industry continues to evolve, broadcast and media teams will need to stay up-to-date with the latest developments in cloud-based technologies and standards, such as ABR, CDN, and OTT, in order to remain competitive and effectively support the growing demand for personalized and targeted advertising. By doing so, they can take advantage of the opportunities presented by cloud-based technologies and develop more efficient, effective, and scalable broadcast workflows that meet the needs of their audiences and advertisers.

items.body_html:
What Was Announced

Telestream has announced a significant advancement in remote production capabilities, dubbed "Remote Production Perfection: From Cloud Capture to Beyond the Edge". This development focuses on streamlining the remote production workflow, allowing teams to capture, process, and distribute content more efficiently. The announcement highlights the ability to automate and scale remote production tasks, reducing operational drag and increasing flexibility for broadcasters.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

This announcement holds significant technical and operational implications for broadcast teams. By enabling cloud-based capture and processing, Telestream's solution addresses a critical pain point in remote production: the need for seamless integration and scalability. The ability to automate and streamline tasks such as ingest, monitoring, and distribution will enable teams to reduce handoffs, improve metadata flow, and accelerate publishing times. Furthermore, this development will allow teams to better predict output under deadline pressure, making it an attractive solution for broadcasters looking to simplify operations while preserving resilience and editorial speed. The underlying technology is likely built upon established standards such as SMPTE ST 2110, which enables the transport of professional media over IP networks. This would allow for the integration of Telestream's solution with existing broadcast infrastructure, reducing the need for costly upgrades or replacements. Additionally, the use of cloud-based processing will enable teams to scale their resources on-demand, reducing the need for expensive hardware investments.

Industry Context

This announcement sits within the broader context of the streaming industry, where buyers and operators are under pressure to increase flexibility without increasing operational drag. Competing technologies, such as those offered by AWS Elemental or Microsoft Azure, are also vying for market share in the remote production space. However, Telestream's solution appears to focus specifically on the needs of broadcast teams, addressing pain points such as scalability, automation, and integration with existing infrastructure. This targeted approach may give Telestream a competitive edge in the market, particularly among broadcasters looking for a more tailored solution. The use of cloud-based processing and automation also aligns with the industry trend towards software-defined infrastructure and the increasing adoption of cloud-based services. This shift is driven by the need for greater flexibility, scalability, and cost-effectiveness in the face of rapidly changing viewer habits and increasing competition in the streaming market.

Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

For broadcast teams, this announcement should be treated as a planning signal rather than a hype signal. Engineers and operations managers should review the architecture and map the dependencies before deciding whether to pilot the solution. A controlled test against a live workflow pain point is likely the best next step, rather than a rushed rollout. By evaluating the change against a real-world bottleneck, teams can determine whether the benefits of Telestream's solution outweigh the costs and risks associated with implementation.

items.dek: What Was Announced A recent analysis has revealed that the environmental benefits of cloud production in broadcasting are more complex than initially claimed...
items.meta_description: The Green Broadcast: Can Hybrid Cloud Workflows Actually Reduce a Station's Carbon Footprint?. What Was Announced A recent analysis has revealed that th...
items.body_html:
What Was Announced

A recent analysis has revealed that the environmental benefits of cloud production in broadcasting are more complex than initially claimed. While cloud production can offer real carbon savings, these benefits are contingent on specific conditions, including the energy efficiency of the broadcaster's existing infrastructure and the location of the cloud data centers processing their workloads. The study highlights the need for honest accounting and rigorous measurement of carbon emissions in broadcast operations.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The findings of this analysis have significant implications for broadcast engineering and operations teams. The study shows that cloud production can deliver substantial carbon savings, particularly in areas such as travel elimination and outside broadcast vehicle reduction. However, these benefits are largely dependent on the ability to defer hardware replacement through cloud migration, thereby avoiding the energy consumption and material extraction associated with hardware manufacture. To achieve genuine sustainability outcomes, broadcasters must adopt hybrid approaches that combine cloud-based workflows with efficient on-premises infrastructure and remote production techniques. The measurement problem in broadcast sustainability is a major obstacle to honest accounting and effective decision-making. The lack of standardized measurement frameworks and methodologies for attributing cloud energy consumption makes it challenging to compare and verify sustainability claims from vendors and service providers. Broadcasters must develop their own measurement capabilities and adopt frameworks like the Albert sustainability certification scheme to ensure accurate and transparent sustainability reporting.

Industry Context

The broadcast industry's adoption of sustainability as a marketing narrative has created a complex landscape of competing claims and technologies. Cloud production, in particular, has been touted as a carbon-neutral solution, but the reality is more nuanced. Other approaches, such as facility consolidation and efficient on-premises infrastructure, can also deliver significant energy savings. The industry is moving towards a more hybrid and flexible approach, with a focus on combining cloud-based workflows with on-premises infrastructure and remote production techniques. This shift is driven by the need for more accurate and transparent sustainability reporting, as well as the growing regulatory demands for corporate sustainability reporting. The regulatory environment is becoming increasingly demanding, with European sustainability reporting requirements expanding in scope and applying to a wider range of organizations. Broadcasters operating in regulated markets must develop genuine measurement capability and honest accounting practices to ensure compliance with these requirements. This concept suggests that the boundaries between traditional broadcast and streaming services are blurring, with a growing trend towards converged workflows that combine the best of both worlds. The Everything Era represents a significant shift in how broadcasters and streaming services approach content delivery. From a technical standpoint, this means that the traditional silos between different workflows – such as playout, ingest, and metadata management – are being dismantled in favor of more integrated and software-defined architectures. This change has the potential to simplify operations, reduce manual handling, and improve the overall efficiency of content delivery. This has led to a growing interest in converged workflows that combine the best of both worlds – the scalability and flexibility of streaming with the reliability and resilience of traditional broadcast systems. Other approaches, such as cloud-native architectures and containerization, are also gaining traction as media companies seek to simplify their operations and reduce costs. Implications for Broadcast and Media Teams

What Was Announced

Avid has announced that its Stream IO ingest and playout solution now supports SMPTE 2110, a standard for professional media over managed IP networks. This development is significant for newsroom teams and broadcast engineers, as it enables the use of IP-based infrastructure for live production and playout workflows. The addition of SMPTE 2110 support to Stream IO is a notable enhancement, as it allows for the transport of uncompressed video and audio over IP networks, providing a more flexible and scalable alternative to traditional SDI-based infrastructure.

The Engineering and Operational Significance

The support for SMPTE 2110 in Avid's Stream IO solution is technically significant because it enables the use of IP-based infrastructure for live production and playout workflows, allowing for greater flexibility and scalability. This development solves the problem of transporting high-quality, uncompressed video and audio signals over IP networks, which is a critical requirement for live broadcast applications. By supporting SMPTE 2110, Stream IO can now integrate with other IP-based devices and systems, enabling the creation of more efficient and flexible workflows. For example, this could allow for the use of IP-based monitoring and distribution systems, such as those using AES67 for audio over IP, to be integrated with the Stream IO solution.

The adoption of SMPTE 2110 is part of a broader industry trend towards the use of IP-based infrastructure for broadcast and media applications. Other vendors, such as Grass Valley and Sony, have also announced support for SMPTE 2110 in their products, demonstrating the growing importance of this standard. This convergence of broadcast and IT technologies is driving the development of new solutions and architectures, such as cloud-based playout and OTT delivery systems, which are increasingly being used by broadcasters and media companies to deliver content to consumers. By carefully evaluating the use of Stream IO with SMPTE 2110, broadcast and media teams can make informed decisions about how to leverage this technology to improve their workflows and deliver high-quality content to their audiences.
